### The Office of Small Recoveries

The office appeared between the bakery and the locksmith on a Tuesday morning. Nobody had seen anyone carry in furniture or paint the door, and the owner of the bakery insisted that the space had been a brick wall the day before. The locksmith disagreed, though he could not say what had occupied it previously. Above the door hung a modest sign:

**OFFICE OF SMALL RECOVERIES**

Underneath, in smaller letters: *Lost things considered.*

By noon, three people had come inside. The first wanted a silver earring. The second had misplaced the receipt for a washing machine. The third, a boy of perhaps nine, stood at the counter and said, “I lost my courage on the way to school.”

The woman behind the counter, whose name was Mara, opened a drawer. It contained pencils, paper clips, a box of matches, and a small brass bell. She rang the bell once.

“Where were you when you last had it?” she asked.

“At home,” the boy said.

“And when did you notice it was gone?”

“Outside the school gate.”

Mara wrote this down on a yellow card. “What happened between home and the gate?”

The boy studied his shoes. “I had to walk past some older kids.”

“Did they say anything to you?”

“One of them asked where I was going with my funny little lunch box.”

“And what did you do?”

“I went inside.”

Mara put down her pencil. “That sounds like courage to me.”

The boy considered this. He did not look entirely convinced, but he accepted the card she gave him. On it she had written: *Item may still be in owner’s possession. Please check again tomorrow.*

The woman with the washing-machine receipt was less satisfied. Mara helped her search her bag and called the shop, which found a record of the purchase. The earring remained missing, though Mara took the customer’s number in case it turned up.

Word spread. By Friday, the office had a queue.

Some visitors brought ordinary problems: keys, umbrellas, a dog that had escaped through a garden gate. Mara kept a map of the town on the wall and marked the places where things had last been seen. She also kept a list of useful telephone numbers, lent out a torch, and learned that the bus depot accumulated an astonishing number of single gloves.

Other requests were harder to record. A man wanted the tune his mother used to hum while making soup. A retired teacher wanted the pleasure she once took in reading novels. A woman asked for the afternoon she had wasted arguing with her sister, who was now dead.

Mara did not promise to find everything. She had a stamp that said *POSSIBLY UNRECOVERABLE*, and she used it when she had to. But she disliked reaching for it too quickly.

For the man who remembered his mother’s humming, she wrote down every detail he could recall: the soup, the flat where he had grown up, the years his mother might have heard the song on the radio. He came back with his aunt the next day. Between them, they sang fragments of six different tunes, none quite right. On the third visit, his aunt recognized one and supplied the missing notes. The man sang it through twice, smiling, then asked if he could sit in the office a little longer.

The retired teacher was annoyed when Mara suggested trying a shorter book.

“I have read all my life,” she said.

“I know,” said Mara. “But you haven’t enjoyed it lately.”

The teacher borrowed a slim mystery from the library. She returned to report that the plot was ridiculous, the detective was conceited, and she had stayed awake until two in the morning to find out who did it.

As autumn arrived, the office became a place where people lingered even after their business was done. The baker sent over unsold rolls. The locksmith repaired a cabinet whose door would not shut. Someone donated a kettle, and someone else brought in a chair that looked uncomfortable but proved to be ideal for waiting.

Mara began to need help. The boy with the lunch box, whose name was Eli, came by after school to sharpen pencils and sort the yellow cards. He was good at noticing connections. When two people reported seeing the missing dog near the river, he suggested asking the anglers who gathered there early in the morning. One of them had been feeding her scraps.

Eli also noticed that Mara never wrote a card for herself.

“Have you ever lost anything?” he asked.

“Plenty.”

“Why don’t you put it in the drawer?”

Mara looked at the drawer. “I suppose I don’t know where to start.”

Eli waited. He had learned that waiting was part of the work.

“At my old job,” Mara said, “I used to make things. Little wooden animals, mostly. For a toy shop.”

“What happened?”

“The shop closed. I found other work, and then I stopped making them.”

“Do you want them back?”

“I gave most of them away.”

“I mean, do you want to make them again?”

Mara said she didn’t know. She was busy, and her hands had grown stiff, and she no longer had her tools. Eli wrote these objections down on a yellow card. Underneath them, he added: *Ask locksmith about tools.*

The locksmith had a carving knife he no longer used. He brought it over with a block of soft wood and refused payment. For several evenings Mara left both items untouched on the counter. Then, after closing one night, she sat beneath the lamp and began to carve.

The result was supposed to be a fox. One ear was too large, and the tail looked more like a bent spoon. Mara almost threw it away. Instead, she put it on the windowsill beside the kettle.

The next morning, Eli picked it up.

“What is it?” he asked.

“A fox.”

He turned it over in his hands. “Can I make one too?”

After that, Mara brought in a second knife, and on quiet afternoons they carved together. She showed Eli how to hold the wood steady and cut away from his fingers. He showed her an easier way to draw patterns with the office’s dull pencils. Neither of them produced anything fit for a toy shop, but by winter the windowsill held a fox, two birds, a lopsided dog, and something Eli called a sea monster.

People still came to the office with things they had lost. Mara still filled out cards, made calls, and marked places on the map. Sometimes a case took weeks; sometimes it ended with the stamp she disliked. When that happened, she would file the card and make a note to ask again if she thought of somewhere else to look.

On the last working day before the holidays, the baker came in carrying a tin of biscuits. She stopped at the windowsill and picked up the fox.

“I like this one,” she said.

“You can have it,” Mara told her.

The baker took it next door and placed it behind the counter, where customers could see it among the jars of sweets. A few days later, someone asked where she had bought it. She pointed toward the office, then added that she didn’t know whether Mara was making any more.

She went over after closing time to ask. Mara was at the counter, turning a piece of wood in her hands.

“I think so,” she said.
